questions.q: What is the common API lifecycle shape shared by major quantum cloud providers, as described in the lesson?
options: Each provider has a completely unrelated lifecycle with no common pattern at all
A synchronous call-and-block model identical to calling a local function
Asynchronous submit(circuit) -> job_id, then poll(job_id) -> status, then get_result(job_id) -- because a job can queue for seconds to hours
Submitting a job always returns the final result immediately with no queueing
questions.explain: Because queue times vary widely and can be long, every major provider uses an asynchronous submit-then-poll (or subscribe) lifecycle rather than a blocking call -- orchestration code must be built around this from the start.

questions.q: How does IBM Quantum's dominant cost unit differ from AWS Braket's?
options: IBM charges nothing for compute; only Braket charges money
IBM bills primarily by wall-clock runtime seconds, while Braket bills by a per-task fee plus a per-shot fee
Both providers bill using an identical per-shot formula
Braket bills by runtime seconds; IBM bills by shot count
questions.explain: Braket's cost scales with (tasks, shots); IBM's Pay-As-You-Go pricing scales with billable runtime seconds -- a fundamentally different pricing dimension that a cost-estimation adapter must account for.

questions.q: Why should orchestration code check a device's status and calibration metadata before submitting a job, according to the lesson?
options: Metadata checks replace the need for any retry logic
Device metadata is required by law before any quantum job can run
It's a cheap, zero-cost check that can prevent submitting an expensive, slow job to a device that's offline, mid-recalibration, or has a long queue -- all of which degrade or waste the submission
Checking metadata guarantees the job will never fail
questions.explain: Device metadata (queue depth, operational status, calibration data) is available before submission at no cost -- skipping it risks submitting to a degraded or backlogged device when that information could have redirected the job.

questions.q: Why can't the abstraction layer's estimate_cost() method use a single shared formula like 'shots x price_per_shot' across all providers?
options: Because shots are never a billing factor for any provider
Because all providers already charge an identical flat rate regardless of usage
Because estimate_cost() is not actually a useful method for any provider

Because providers bill on different pricing dimensions -- Braket on tasks/shots, IBM on runtime seconds -- so the adapter behind estimate_cost() needs provider-specific logic even though the caller's interface stays the same
questions.explain: The complexity of translating between pricing dimensions (shots vs. runtime seconds) has to live inside each provider's adapter, so that calling code can call one consistent estimate_cost(circuit, shots) interface regardless of which provider is actually selected.

questions.q: What is the key difference between how 'program sets' (AWS Braket) and Qiskit Runtime 'primitives/sessions' (IBM) serve a similar purpose?
options: Both batch multiple circuit executions to amortize overhead -- Braket's program sets share one per-task fee across circuits, while IBM's primitives/sessions batch executions within a runtime session
Only Azure Quantum offers any form of batching
They are unrelated features that serve completely different, unconnected purposes
Program sets and sessions both eliminate queueing entirely
questions.explain: Both mechanisms exist to batch related circuit executions and reduce per-execution overhead, but they map onto each provider's own pricing/session model differently -- exactly the kind of provider-specific behavior the abstraction layer needs to understand.
